title: The Extra Girl
byline: Mack Sennett Productions · F. Richard Jones (dir.) · Mabel Normand · Associated Exhibitors, 1923

evidence.note: US film, copyright registered November 9, 1923 by Mack Sennett/Associated Exhibitors. Maximum statutory term—28-year initial term plus 67-year renewal extension under the Sonny Bono CTEA—equals 95 years, expiring December 31, 2018. The 1923 print entered US public domain on January 1, 2019; as of 2026 the 1930-or-earlier bright line applies unconditionally.
evidence.source: US Copyright Office Circular 15a — Duration of Copyright

evidence.note: Silent film: the 1923 print has no original recorded soundtrack. Any musical score present on a modern transfer is a separately protected work. Kino International's DVD edition adds a newly composed score alongside new intertitles (© 2008 Kino International Corp.); Flicker Alley's Blu-ray release similarly packages a modern score. Those added scores are protected works independent of the underlying PD footage. The Internet Archive transfer (archived May 2013, identifier THEEXTRAGIRL1923MabelNormandRalphGravesGeorgeNichols) does not carry a licensing notice for an added score, but any audio on any modern copy should be evaluated before use.
evidence.source: Kino Lorber EDU — Mabel Normand: The Extra Girl and The Gusher

evidence.note: Original story conceived by Mack Sennett; screenplay by Bernard McConville. No adaptation from any prior published work has been identified—this is an original scenario created for the 1923 production. First published with the film's release October 28, 1923. The same 95-year maximum term applies; the underlying story entered US public domain on January 1, 2019.
evidence.source: US Copyright Office Circular 15a — Duration of Copyright

evidence.note: A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.

Kino International DVD (c. 2008) bears 'New titles © 2008 Kino International Corp.' and includes a commissioned musical score—both elements are protected independently of the 1923 footage and remain so through at least 2103. Flicker Alley has released a Blu-ray edition of Mack Sennett material that includes this film; that release carries its own protected restoration creative additions (score, intertitle design). Using footage sourced from either commercial release without licensing their specific creative contributions is infringement even though the underlying footage is public domain.

editorial:
The Extra Girl is a five-reel Mack Sennett silent comedy released by Associated Exhibitors on October 28, 1923—the last feature Mabel Normand completed with Sennett and the last major picture of her career. Directed by F. Richard Jones from an original screenplay by Bernard McConville, it casts Normand as Sue Graham, a small-town girl who wins a studio talent contest but is assigned to the wardrobe department rather than the camera, until a lion she accidentally unleashes on the backlot provides the film's signature set-piece. Copyright was registered November 9, 1923; even under the maximum possible statutory term (28-year initial plus 67-year CTEA extension = 95 years), the 1923 print expired December 31, 2018 and entered US public domain on January 1, 2019. The underlying footage and original story are free to stream, excerpt, remix, license, and sell.

The practical rights trap is layered onto modern copies, not onto the 1923 footage itself. Kino International's DVD edition carries new intertitles © 2008 Kino International Corp. and a commissioned musical score; Flicker Alley's Blu-ray release adds its own protected creative elements. The new intertitles and scores in both editions are protected independently through at least 2103; a faithful restoration of the underlying footage itself adds no new US copyright. Producers who want to use this film without a license should source from the Internet Archive transfer (archived May 2013, identifier THEEXTRAGIRL1923MabelNormandRalphGravesGeorgeNichols), which predates the commercial releases and carries no copyright-protected additions, then supply an original or public-domain score. Ripping footage directly from a Kino or Flicker Alley copy-protected disc can trigger DMCA anti-circumvention liability independent of any copyright question, even for a public-domain film; any audio track from those editions must also be licensed separately from the footage.
faq: Can I use the Kino DVD version of The Extra Girl in my documentary?

Not without a license for Kino's additions. The 1923 footage is public domain—a faithful restoration of it adds no new US copyright—but the Kino DVD includes new intertitles (© 2008 Kino International Corp.) and a commissioned musical score, both of which are protected independently of the film itself. Ripping the copy-protected disc also raises DMCA anti-circumvention concerns separate from copyright. Source your footage from the Internet Archive transfer instead and supply your own score or public-domain music.
Can I sell a VOD or physical release built around The Extra Girl?

Yes, using the underlying 1923 footage from a public-domain source such as the Internet Archive transfer. You cannot replicate the Kino or Flicker Alley editions because their new intertitles and scores are protected original additions—a faithful restoration of the footage itself adds no new US copyright, but those creative elements do—and ripping their copy-protected discs can trigger DMCA liability. Add your own title cards and score, and the print and story layers are clear—though verify current right-of-publicity law in your target jurisdiction regarding Mabel Normand's likeness in commercial contexts.
